messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: User-defined covariates as detection parameters in camera/telemetry models
parts:
Hi Luciano

I think you are expecting too much of 'secr' and your data. You have only one animal with telemetry data and that was not detected at a camera - how can that individual represent the behaviour of the whole population? As usual, I am averse to combining capture-recapture and telemetry. You are free to play 'what if...' games by estimating sigma from the telemetry data and fixing sigma to that value in the capture-recapture analysis; that keeps the logic clean, but I wouldn't get excited about the result.

'secr' does not model detection as a function of landscape (mask) covariates (but you can associate covariates with detectors). It seems that your covariates have a large number of levels (indicated by " c,m,t combinations exceed..."), which demands a lot of memory in 'secr'. You could try collapsing those covariates into fewer discrete values.

I think you have 32 detections of 10 animals, and that is at the lower limit of what is required for any (spatial) capture-recapture model. I doubt there is power to distinguish among more fancy models, so I wouldn't go there.

Of course, others may see this differently.

Murray

messages.subject: Re: User-defined covariates as detection parameters in camera/telemetry models
parts:
Hi Murray, 

thanks for all the clarifications and the rationale behind the limits of one telemetered animal. 
I can try to collapse the values in discrete breaks as suggested, to see if at least the issue gets solved for future similar uses. 

We tried also to model density as a function of Euclidean and non-Euclidean models. You point that 10 animals is on the very low end of a minimum sample size requirement for any spatial capture-recapture study. Can this be a reason on why, in these evaluations, the null model has the strongest AICc-based support? Our species is dependent on ruggedness and elevation, captures are clustered towards certain areas with particular topographical characteristics, but still these do not seem to influence density (on our dataset) in any of the ways we have evaluated.

Thanks again,

Luciano

messages.subject: Re: User-defined covariates as detection parameters in camera/telemetry models
parts: When you think about it, it's hard to distinguish the pattern of 10 dots on a map from a random (Poisson) distribution, plus you don't even know where each of those dots really is. This is radically different to a resource selection model for telemetry locations, for which you likely have a large sample and the locations are known. But of course the RSF relates to habitat selection of a different order sensu Johnson 1980.
